listenings.text: I read about twenty of these requests a week, and I can tell you in ten seconds which ones I can fill. The ones I can fill have a sentence after the job title. Not three paragraphs, one sentence. A piping engineer who has worked on food plants. A structural engineer whose foundation drawings we can issue without a review. That sentence is the whole search. Without it, I have forty names and no way to choose, so I write back and ask, and we lose a week. The other thing I need is the honest date. People give me a date that is two weeks earlier than the real one, because they think I will be late. Then I move somebody off another project to hit a date that did not exist, and now two teams are unhappy. Give me the sentence and the real date, and most requests close in two days.

I spent three months in Brazil on a secondment, and the work itself was the easy part. What nobody planned was my own desk in Helsinki. On paper somebody was going to cover my drawings, but that person already had a full workload, so for three months my old project ran with no piping lead. Nothing failed immediately. Things just got slower, and then a question about a pump base waited eleven days for an answer. When I came back, I had two projects to catch up with instead of one. So now, when a colleague tells me about a secondment, the first thing I ask is not where or how long. I ask who is backfilling, and whether that person has been told, because being told in the first week of the assignment is not the same as being asked in advance.

reading.rtitle: How a Multi-Office Project Gets Staffed
paras: Every project manager has written the same email: we need a structural engineer and a piping engineer by the fifteenth. Almost every one of those emails comes back with a question, because a job title describes a category and a project needs a person. The resource managers who read these requests all day say the same thing: give us the sentence after the title.

The sentence after the title is the one that narrows the search. A piping engineer who has worked on food plants is a different person from one whose experience is all in oil and gas. An engineer whose drawings can be issued without a review is worth two who need checking. And the package that worries you most should get the seniority, even if a junior could technically do the work, because the interfaces are where projects fail and interfaces need judgement.

The second half of the problem is the office the person leaves behind. A secondment that is agreed in a hurry usually creates a hole somewhere else, and nobody asks who backfills the role until the first week of the assignment. Good resourcing asks the question early, and it accepts an honest answer: if the headcount is frozen and nobody can backfill, then the project cannot mobilize that person, and the plan has to change while there is still time to change it.

reading.prompt: What is the main idea of the text?
choices: Job titles are enough to find the right engineer if you send the request early.
A staffing request only works when it adds the detail that narrows the search, and when it asks early who will backfill the role the person leaves.
Junior engineers should always be given the most difficult interfaces.

items: According to the text, a job title is enough to find the right person.
